In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] theory of [[Lie group]]s, the '''Chevalley restriction theorem''' describes functions on a [[Lie algebra]] which are invariant under the [[group action|action]] of a Lie group in terms of functions on a [[Cartan subalgebra]].

==Statement==
Chevalley's theorem requires the following notation:
{| class="wikitable"
!  !! assumption !! example
|-
| ''G'' || complex connected [[semisimple Lie group]] || SL<sub>''n''</sub>, the [[special linear group]]
|-
| <math>\mathfrak g</math> || the Lie algebra of ''G'' || <math>\mathfrak{sl}_n</math>, the Lie algebra of matrices with [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] zero
|-
| <math>\mathbb C[\mathfrak g]^G</math> || the polynomial functions on <math>\mathfrak g</math> which are invariant under the [[adjoint action|adjoint ''G''-action]]||
|-
| <math>\mathfrak h</math> || a Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math> || the subalgebra of [[diagonal matrices]] with trace 0
|-
| ''W'' || the [[Weyl group]] of ''G'' || the [[symmetric group]] S<sub>''n''</sub>
|-
| <math>\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]^W</math> || the polynomial functions on <math>\mathfrak h</math> which are invariant under the natural action of ''W'' || polynomials ''f'' on the space <math>\{x_1, \dots, x_n , \sum x_i =0 \}</math> which are invariant under all permutations of the ''x''<sub>''i''</sub>
|}

'''Chevalley's theorem''' asserts that the restriction of polynomial functions induces an [[isomorphism]]
:<math>\mathbb C[\mathfrak g]^{G} \cong \mathbb C[\mathfrak h]^{W}</math>.

==Proofs==
{{harvtxt|Humphreys|1980}} gives a [[mathematical proof|proof]] using properties of representations of highest weight. {{harvtxt|Chriss|Ginzburg|2010}} give a proof of Chevalley's theorem exploiting the geometric properties of the map <math>\widetilde \mathfrak g := G \times_B \mathfrak b \to \mathfrak g</math>.

This theorem in fact more generally holds for any reductive Lie algebra, and can also be proved directly in the case that <math>G = \mathrm{GL}_n</math>. In this case, the Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{t}</math> can be identified with diagonal matrices, and the Weyl group can be identified with the symmetric group acting on diagonal matrices by permutations. Therefore, <math>\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{t}] \cong \mathbb{C}[x_1, ..., x_n]</math> and <math>\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{t}]^W</math> can be identified with the subring of <math>\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{t}]</math> generated by <math>e_1, ..., e_n</math> where each <math>e_i</math> is an [[elementary symmetric polynomial]]. 

Identify <math>\mathfrak g</math> with the set of <math>n \times n</math> matrices. For injectivity, if we are given a <math>G</math>-invariant polynomial on <math>\mathfrak g</math> which vanishes on the set of diagonal matrices, by <math>G</math>-invariance, this polynomial vanishes on any matrix which is conjugate to a diagonal matrix. Since these elements are Zariski dense in <math>\mathfrak g</math>, this polynomial vanishes on a Zariski dense open subset of <math>\mathfrak g</math> and thus must itself be the zero polynomial. 

For surjectivity, it of course suffices to show that each <math>e_i</math> lies in the image of this map. Using [[Newton's identities]] and an inductive argument, it suffices to prove that the function <math>x_1^i + ... + x_n^i</math> lies in the image of this map for every <math>i \in \{1, ..., n\}</math>. However, in this case, one can explicitly construct an invariant function which restricts to <math>x_1^i + ... + x_n^i</math> on diagonal matrices: it is given by the function <math>A \mapsto \mathrm{trace}(A^i)</math>.
